'''Frank Klaus Tittel''' (November 14, 1933 – February 17, 2026) was a German-born British-American [[laser]] physicist, engineer and inventor, who was J.S. Abercrombie Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering at [[Rice University]]. He was best known for his contributions to [[tunable laser]]s and [[laser absorption spectrometry]], as well as for the invention of quartz-enhanced photoacoustic absorption spectroscopy.

==Biography==
Tittel was born on November 14, 1933, in [[Oranienburg]], Germany. His father was an industrial chemist while his mother was [[History of the Jews in Germany|Jewish]]. In 1941, his father died in a skiing accident, while his brother died from an ear infection after being denied medical care due to his heritage. His mother committed suicide in the same year, after their family home was [[Aryanization|seized]] by the [[Nazi Party]]. During the [[World War II]], he lived with various foster families and in a Czechoslovak camp for orphaned children. In 1948, he moved to England to live with his aunt.<ref name="rice-memoriam"/><ref name="spie-memoriam"/>

Tittel earned bachelor's and doctoral degrees in physics from [[University of Oxford]] in 1955 and 1959, respectively. In 1960, he emigrated to the United States to work as a research scientist with [[General Electric]], where he worked on the recently introduced [[ruby laser]]s. Following a short tenure at The [[American University in Cairo]], he joined the [[Rice University]] as an associate professor in 1967 and was promoted to a full professor in 1973. Named the J.S. Abercrombie Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering in 1989, he led the Rice Quantum Institute from 1996 to 2000. Tittel died on February 17, 2026, and was survived by his wife, Maria, as well as by his two sons and two grandchildren.<ref name="rice-memoriam"/>

During his tenure at Rice University, Tittel pioneered [[tunable laser]]s, which became a breakthrough in laser spectroscopy. He collaborated closely with [[Robert Curl]] and [[Richard Smalley]]; his contributions were instrumental in the discovery of [[buckminsterfullerene]], for which Curl and Smalley was awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] in 1996. In 2002, he co-invented quartz-enhanced photoacoustic absorption spectroscopy,<ref name="kosterev2002"/> which was eventually used in the [[multi-component gas analyzer system]]s of [[NASA]].<ref name="rice-memoriam"/> He was elected a Fellow of [[Optica (society)|Optica]] in 1987 for "contributions to the [[excimer laser]] and laser spectroscopy."<ref name="optica-memoriam"/> He became a Fellow of [[SPIE]] in 2014, and was also a fellow of the [[IEEE]] and the [[American Physical Society]].<ref name="spie-memoriam"/> He was awarded the [[IEEE Medal for Environmental and Safety Technologies]] alongside [[Jérôme Faist]] in 2018 for "his pioneering contributions to optical chemical sensors."<ref name="optica-memoriam"/><ref name="eth"/>
